source_text: CAPUT UNDECIMUM, De immutabilitate Dei. Adhuc fuit tertium Dei attributum, nempe simplicitas: sequitur quartum, nimirum immutabilitas, quae est summa Dei perfectio, qua semper manet idem, qui est. IMMUTABILITAS, quam Graeci quidam atrepsian reddunt, e sacris literis non disertim, sed similibus et oppositis potentiae vocibus exprimitur.
english: CHAPTER ELEVEN. On the immutability of God.

Thus far there has been the third attribute of God, namely simplicity: there follows the fourth, namely immutability, which is God's highest perfection, by which He always remains the same who He is. IMMUTABILITY, which certain Greeks render as unchangeableness, is expressed from the sacred letters not by a distinct word, but by like and opposite words of power.

source_text: Similis potentiae est, quod de Deo affirmatur Psal. CII.27. Tu autem permanes. Et 28. Tu vero idem es. Et Malach. III.6. Non mutor. Sic Rom. I.23. dicitur aphthartos Theos, incorruptibilis Deus. I Tim. VI.16. Qui solus habet immortalitatem. Oppositae potentiae voces de eo negantur Iac. I.17. Apud quem non est transmutatio aut conversionis obumbratio. Materiale etiam in hoc attributo idem est quod in caeteris, scilicet eminentissima Dei perfectio. Formalis vero illius ratio consistit in negatione omnis mutationis, per quam Deus in essentia sua aliud atque aliud fiat. Neque enim unquam novam perfectionem acquirit, neque illam quam possidet amittit.
english: It is of like power that of God it is affirmed in Psalm 102:27, But You remain. And in verse 28, But You are the same. And Malachi 3:6, I do not change. So Romans 1:23 says the incorruptible God. 1 Timothy 6:16, who alone has immortality. Opposite words of power are denied of Him in James 1:17: with whom there is no change or shadow of turning.

The material in this attribute also is the same as in the rest, namely God's most eminent perfection. But its formal ratio consists in the negation of every change by which God in His essence would become other and other. For He never acquires a new perfection, nor loses that which He possesses.

source_text: Deum vero in se plane immutabilem esse, hunc in modum ostendo. PRIMO, ob eminentissimam illius unitatem. Quicquid eminentissime unum est, id est in se plane immutabile. Atqui Deus eminentissime unus est, ut demonstratum hujus libri cap. IV. Ergo Deus est in se plane immutabilis. SECUNDO, ab absoluta existendi necessitate. Quicquid absoluta necessitate existit, id in se plane immutabile est. Atqui Deus absoluta necessitate existit, ut demonstratum est cap. VIII. TERTIO, ab infinita essentiae perfectione. Quicquid infinita est perfectione praeditum, id in se plane est immutabile. QUARTO, a simplicitate. Quicquid est absolute simplex, id in se plane est immutabile, quia nullius accidentis capax est. Atqui Deus est absolute simplex, ut demonstratum est cap. X.
english: That God is in Himself plainly immutable I show in this way. FIRST, from His most eminent unity. Whatever is most eminently one is in itself plainly immutable. But God is most eminently one, as was demonstrated in chapter IV of this book. Therefore God is in Himself plainly immutable.

SECOND, from the absolute necessity of existing. Whatever exists by absolute necessity is in itself plainly immutable. But God exists by absolute necessity, as was demonstrated in chapter VIII. THIRD, from the infinite perfection of essence. Whatever is endowed with infinite perfection is in itself plainly immutable. FOURTH, from simplicity. Whatever is absolutely simple is in itself plainly immutable, because it is capable of no accident. But God is absolutely simple, as was demonstrated in chapter X.

source_text: QUINTO, ab inductione modorum, quibus natura intelligens mutari potest: quod ad existentiam; ad accidentia; ad cognitionem; ad decretum sive propositum voluntatis. Atqui nullo horum modorum Deus mutatur. SEXTO, ab independentia. Qui est independens, is in se plane immutabilis est. Atqui Deus est independens, ut probatum est cap. V. SEPTIMO, a statu entis in potentia. Quicquid est mutabile, id aliquo modo in potentia est. Atqui Deus nullo modo in potentia est. Actus purus, imo purissimus, solus Deus est. OCTAVO, a natura motus. A quo omnis motus et mutatio est, id est simpliciter immobile atque immutabile, ut Augustinus et Boethius ex Aristotele asserunt. Atqui a Deo est omnis motus ac mutatio.
english: FIFTH, from an induction of the modes by which an intelligent nature can be changed: as to existence; as to accidents; as to knowledge; as to decree or purpose of will. But by none of these modes is God changed. SIXTH, from independence. Whoever is independent is in Himself plainly immutable. But God is independent, as was proved in chapter V.

SEVENTH, from the state of a being in potency. Whatever is mutable is somehow in potency. But God is in no way in potency. Pure act, indeed the purest, is God alone. EIGHTH, from the nature of motion. That from which every motion and change is, is simply immobile and immutable, as Augustine and Boethius assert from Aristotle. But from God is every motion and change.

source_text: CONRADUS VORSTIUS Notis ad disp. III. de DEO hoc attributum Dei aliquo modo inficias ire videtur, scribens quintam speciem mutationis eatenus in Deo locum habere posse, quatenus ipse actiones quasdam immanentes exercet juxta liberam voluntatem. Sed antiquitus dubia quaedam orthodoxo consensui objecta fuerunt a scholasticis: 1. quod Deus inceperit agere; 2. quod heri sciverit solem hodie oriturum; 3. quod tolleretur libertas ejus si non posset mutare voluntatem; 4. quod factus sit homo; 5. quod Deus sit mutatus quia passus et mortuus. SINGULA haec argumenta infra habent propriam sedem. Interim cum certum sit Deum esse penitus immutabilem et immobilem, paucae hic observandae sunt regulae ad contrariorum argumentorum solutionem utiles.
english: Conrad Vorstius in his Notes on Disputation III On God seems somehow to deny this attribute of God, writing that the fifth species of change can have a place in God insofar as He exercises certain immanent actions according to free will.

But of old certain doubts were objected to the orthodox consensus by the scholastics: first, that God began to act; second, that yesterday He knew the sun would rise today; third, that His liberty would be taken away if He could not change His will; fourth, that He was made man; fifth, that God was changed because He suffered and died. Each of these arguments has its proper seat below. Meanwhile, since it is certain that God is entirely immutable and immobile, a few rules are here to be observed, useful for solving contrary arguments.

source_text: REGULAE. 1. Mutatio proprie est secundum substantiam, motus autem secundum accidens. Unde, cum Deus nec in substantia neque in formis accidentalibus in potentia sit, omnino immutabilis est. 2. Deus se movere dicitur per effectum naturae, vel gratiae, vel gloriae; talis motus ad Deum non refertur, sed ad ejus effectum. 3. Deus motu mundum gubernat, qui ab ipso est, non qui in ipso est; praepositio in, cum dicitur incommutabilis, non privat eum potentia movendi active, sed negat potentiam mobilitatis passivae. 4. Motus appropinquationis et elongationis non referuntur ad Deum, nisi secundum effectum. 5. Non aliter se nunc habet Deus, quam ab aeterno; creator et conservator dicitur per relationem quae eum duntaxat extrinsecus denominat. 6. Ex habitu ad actum non mutantur nisi ea quae ita agunt ut pati possint. 7. Cum Deus dicitur nunc velle quod prius non voluit, id dicit mutationem in volito, non in volente. 8. Alia est ratio relationis personalis in divinis, quam aliarum relationum in creaturis.
english: RULES. 1. Change properly is according to substance, but motion according to accident. Hence, since God is in potency neither in substance nor in accidental forms, He is altogether immutable. 2. God is said to move Himself by an effect of nature, or of grace, or of glory; such motion is not referred to God, but to His effect. 3. God governs the world by a motion which is from Him, not which is in Him; the preposition in, when He is called unchangeable, does not deprive Him of active power of moving, but denies passive power of being moved.

4. Motions of approach and withdrawal are not referred to God except according to effect. 5. God does not now hold Himself otherwise than from eternity; He is called creator and conserver by a relation that denominates Him only extrinsically. 6. From habit to act only those are changed which so act that they can suffer. 7. When God is said now to will what He did not will before, that says a change in the thing willed, not in the one willing. 8. The ratio of personal relation in the divine is other than that of other relations in creatures.

source_text: 9. Deus semper idem est ratione essentiae, intellectus, voluntatis et potentiae suae, Psal. CII.27,28. 10. Deum poenitet, non quod mutet consilia, sed beneficia et judicia sua, sicut ea mutare decrevit. 11. Quae Deus sub conditione decernit, praecipit, promittit, comminatur, vel agit, ea arguunt ipsius libertatem, bonitatem, vel severitatem, non vero mutabilitatem. 12. Deus non dependet a creaturis, sed decernit se aliquid facturum per creaturas et circa eas. 13. Deus creando, redimendo et alia faciendo extra se, non mutatur, sed omnipotentiam, clementiam et justitiam suam libere applicat variis objectis. 14. Deus ex irato fit placatus et vicissim, non per mutationem essentiae, sed per commutationem judicii cum beneficio. 15. Preces, sanctitas et mala vita, non mutant Deum, sed opera Dei secundum decretum ejus. 16. Immutabilitas Dei facit ad fidem, ne id habeamus pro Deo quod mutatur; ad consolationem, ut persuasum habeamus Deum nunquam mutaturum suam erga nos benevolentiam; ad pietatem, ut simus et nos constantes immutabiles in amore Dei et proximi.
english: 9. God is always the same by reason of His essence, intellect, will, and power in Psalm 102:27-28. 10. God repents, not because He changes counsels, but benefits and judgments, as He decreed to change them. 11. What God under condition decrees, commands, promises, threatens, or does, argues His liberty, goodness, or severity, not mutability. 12. God does not depend on creatures, but decrees that He will do something through creatures and about them.

13. God, by creating, redeeming, and doing other things outside Himself, is not changed, but freely applies His omnipotence, clemency, and justice to various objects. 14. God from angry becomes placated and vice versa, not by change of essence, but by exchange of judgment with benefit. 15. Prayers, holiness, and evil life do not change God, but the works of God according to His decree. 16. The immutability of God serves faith, lest we take for God what changes; consolation, that we may be persuaded God will never change His goodwill toward us; and piety, that we too may be constant and immutable in the love of God and neighbor.
